title: Diverge, Then Converge With Evidence
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Diverge, Then Converge With Evidence. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Divergence is valuable when it changes assumptions, mechanisms, or system boundaries. It can reopen the problem frame as well as the solution. Teams should diverge at four levels:

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at divergence changes the decision space?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: explanations: competing accounts of why the current outcome occurs; opportunities: different moments or actors where intervention could matter; mechanisms: prevention, information, capability, incentive, policy, automation, human judgement, or recovery; representations: alternative ways to enact and test promising mechanisms.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Convergence is not voting. It is a sequence of evidence-backed commitments under constraint. Some options should be eliminated by a veto condition such as unsafe delegation of clinical judgement. Some need a cheap probe. Some can coexist as a portfolio. Others should remain documented but dormant until an assumption changes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build an option portfolio?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Create one option card per materially different direction. Include the problem explanation, target outcome, mechanism, affected actors, value created, value displaced, dependencies, riskiest assumption, evidence already available, consequence of being wrong, and cheapest discriminating test.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Then use three passes:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Eligibility: remove options that violate non-negotiable safety, accessibility, legal, ethical, or strategic constraints. Challenge habits disguised as constraints. 2. Discrimination: ask what evidence would distinguish the surviving options. Do not fully prototype every one. Test the assumptions most likely to reverse the decision. 3.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Commitment: select a direction, combination, or staged sequence. Record why, residual uncertainty, review triggers, and what would reopen divergence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A weighted matrix can structure discussion but cannot make values objective. Keep vetoes, evidence confidence, and distributional effects outside the averaged score. A design that helps most patients while delaying urgent referrals for a smaller group is not adequately represented by a higher mean score.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: failed delivery?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An ecommerce team might improve address entry, allow landmarks, predict delivery windows, enable courier contact, add pickup points, or change the failed-delivery policy. These options intervene at different causes and moments. Field observation can test address and coordination assumptions; an operations pilot can test pickup capacity.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The decision is a staged system, not the winning screen in a workshop.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Cosmetic portfolio: interface variants masquerade as strategic alternatives. Evidence asymmetry: the familiar option has data while novel options are rejected for uncertainty. Premature feasibility: current architecture becomes an unquestionable boundary. Endless optionality: no decision owner or convergence date exists.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Matrix laundering: contested values disappear inside scores. Sunk-cost defence: evidence changes but the chosen direction remains protected.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Create options at different system levels
turns.text: What changes when we look at create options at different system levels?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: During divergence, ideas are recorded with the opportunity addressed, mechanism, assumptions, and likely harms. Feasibility questions are captured so they are not lost, but they do not let the present system define the entire solution space. Individual generation precedes group sharing to reduce anchoring and hierarchy.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Analogies are translated into principles rather than copied as features.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Convergence occurs in stages. The team first removes options that violate safety or ethics, then compares the rest against patient progress, clinical suitability, continuity, equity, staff capacity, technical feasibility, reversibility, and learning value. Evidence supports the criteria; voting only reveals preference.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Hybrid options are allowed when mechanisms reinforce each other.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: reducing failed delivery?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Options can change address data, courier navigation, recipient communication, building access, pickup policy, or merchant packaging. Diverging only on notification design hides most of the service system. Convergence should compare where each option changes the failure mechanism.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners make optionality affordable. They fund small probes before large commitments, sequence reversible decisions first, and identify one-way doors. They also inspect political dynamics: whose option receives research, whose constraints are believed, and whose labour is displaced.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The record should allow a future team to understand not only what was chosen but which changed condition would make a rejected option relevant again.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at separate expansion from commitment?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Convergence uses visible criteria derived from outcome and risk: patient progress, clinical safety, equity, capacity, evidence quality, reversibility, and learning value. Ideas can combine; attractive concepts can be rejected. The output is a portfolio of assumptions and next tests, not a voting result disguised as strategy.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a team inbox. Complaints about missed messages lead to several ideas: stronger alerts, clearer ownership, a shared triage queue, and fewer notification types. Sketch them before choosing. Then test which approach helps teams assign and resolve real messages without creating a new interruption burden.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Divergence is useful only when convergence uses evidence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find a product that solves a problem mainly through interface friction. List one policy, infrastructure, human-service, and prevention alternative. What organisational assumption made the interface solution appear inevitable?
